questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The first question about a document
questions.learningObjective: State the first question to ask of any historical document
questions.stem: When a historian first encounters a document, what is the first question to ask?

options.text: Who wrote it, when, where, and for what purpose?
Is it old enough to be interesting?
Does it support my thesis?
How long is it?

questions.explanation: Provenance and purpose come first. Age, thesis fit, and length are secondary or distorting questions.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why independent sources strengthen a claim

options.text: More sources always mean the claim is true regardless of quality.
Independent agreement reduces the chance of shared bias or fabrication.
Corroboration only works for written sources, not oral ones.
Independent sources are valuable only when they agree completely.

questions.explanation: Independent sources sharing no common origin make shared bias or fabrication less likely. Quantity alone does not guarantee truth.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a customs register can establish
questions.learningObjective: State what a customs register can and cannot establish

stimulus.body: A port customs register lists ships, cargoes, duties paid, and dates for 1780 to 1820. It records no passengers, no prices, and no destinations beyond the next port.

questions.stem: Given the register, what can it most reliably establish about trade?

The final destination and retail price of every cargo.

options.text: Volumes and duties of goods passing through the port in those years.
Nothing useful, because passenger data are missing.

questions.explanation: The register supports claims about volumes and duties. It cannot establish final destinations, prices, or motives.

answer.exemplar: Each genre has conventions and purposes, so a legal deed proves transfer of property but not feelings, while a diary may reveal motives but not official facts.

questions.explanation: Genre conventions determine what a source was meant to do. A deed proves transfer, not emotion; a diary suggests motive, not official fact.

Dismiss it as obviously evil and ignore its contemporary justification.
Praise it as the best system ever devised.
Explain it within its own political debate rather than simply condemn it by modern standards.

questions.explanation: Historians explain practices within their own context before judging. Pure presentism or uncritical praise both distort understanding.
